question: A patient with a head injury has one pupil that is large and doesn't react well to light. What does this usually suggest?

options.A: An allergic reaction to systemic intravenous antibiotic therapy
options.B: A minor scalp laceration healing normally without complication
options.C: Compression of cranial nerve III due to brain herniation
options.D: Permanent regeneration of damaged peripheral nerve pathways

explanation: When pressure pushes brain tissue downward, it can squeeze cranial nerve III, which controls the pupil. This causes that classic 'fixed and dilated' pupil.

question: What is the main job of androgens (like testosterone) in the normal female body?

options.A: Stopping all activity in the anterior pituitary gland
options.B: Triggering immediate shedding of the uterine lining
options.C: Maintaining thick cervical mucus to block sperm entry
options.D: Supporting bone strength, libido, and serving as a precursor for estrogen

explanation: Even though they're often called 'male' hormones, women have them too! They keep your bones strong, fuel your energy and drive, and help build estrogen.

question: What is the main goal of doing a thoracentesis?

options.A: To clear mucus plugs from the main airways
options.B: To measure pressure inside the right atrium
options.C: To deliver medications directly into the lung tissue
options.D: To remove fluid or air from the pleural space

explanation: You've got this! A thoracentesis simply means putting a tiny needle into the chest cavity to drain out unwanted fluid or air that shouldn't be there.

question: What attitude is most essential for a nurse when assessing a patient with a history of FGM?

options.A: Paternalistic and authoritative
options.B: Skeptical and questioning
options.C: Non-judgmental and culturally sensitive
options.D: Indifferent and strictly clinical

explanation: Patients require a safe, empathetic environment free from moral judgment to discuss sensitive genital trauma openly. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T6#GNS312_U1_T6_h6)

question: Which report from a postpartum mother at home means she needs to see a doctor urgently?

options.A: Experiencing mild fatigue in the late afternoon
options.B: Having pinkish-brown lochia on day ten
options.C: Soaking through more than one sanitary pad in an hour
options.D: Feeling mild muscle soreness from walking

explanation: Soaking a pad or more every single hour is a major warning sign of late postpartum hemorrhage. She needs immediate medical attention!

question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of youth-friendly health services?

options.A: Affordable or free healthcare pricing structures
options.B: Mandatory parental presence for every clinic visit
options.C: Respectful, non-judgmental healthcare staff
options.D: Absolute confidentiality and privacy safeguards

explanation: You got it! Requiring parents to be present for every single visit actually discourages teens from seeking confidential reproductive care.

question: How can community nurses best handle cultural and religious concerns about family planning?

options.A: Refusing to discuss birth control with clients holding traditional views
options.B: Providing respectful, culturally sensitive education and open dialogue
options.C: Reporting hesitant clients to local law enforcement agencies
options.D: Ignoring community concerns and forcing medical rules upon families

explanation: Brilliant! Trust is built when we listen patiently, respect community values, and explain health concepts with kindness and understanding.

question: Which sign is a strong indicator of a catheter-associated urinary tract infection?

options.A: Cloudy and foul-smelling urine
options.B: Extreme dryness of the mouth
options.C: Bright red blood in the stool
options.D: Sudden swelling of the lower legs

explanation: You nailed it! When urine turns cloudy, smells bad, or the patient feels feverish and uncomfortable, it usually points to a brewing infection.

question: A client taking long-term NSAIDs for joint pain reports stomach upset and dark, tarry stools. What should you do first?

options.A: Advise the client to double the fluid intake immediately
options.B: Report the findings promptly to the healthcare provider
options.C: Suggest taking the medication on an entirely empty stomach
options.D: Reassure the client that dark stools are a normal side effect

explanation: Dark, tarry stools are a telltale sign of bleeding in the gut (GI bleed), a serious side effect of long-term NSAID use. Always report this right away!

question: What is the primary job of the large intestine in the human body?

options.A: Digesting complex fats and proteins
options.B: Filtering waste products out of the blood stream
options.C: Producing most of the body's digestive enzymes
options.D: Absorbing water and forming stool

explanation: The main function of the colon is to take liquid chyme from the small intestine, absorb the water and electrolytes, and turn it into solid feces. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T9#GNS213_U3_T9_h1)

question: What is the minimum number of generations a nurse should typically explore when taking a family health history?

options.A: Five generations
options.B: Only one generation
options.C: Three generations
options.D: Ten generations

explanation: Looking back across three generations (parents, children, and grandparents) helps reveal hidden inheritance patterns of hereditary conditions. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T15#GNS311_U1_T15_h3)

question: A 55-year-old patient has a 10-year history of poorly controlled high blood pressure. What major condition are they at high risk for?

options.A: Chronic kidney stones
options.B: Cerebrovascular accident
options.C: Iron deficiency anemia
options.D: Degenerative joint disease

explanation: You nailed it! Years of high pressure wear down cerebral blood vessels, putting the patient at high risk for a stroke (cerebrovascular accident).

question: What should you do immediately if a patient says a warm compress feels like it is burning their skin?

options.A: Press the compress down harder to ensure even contact
options.B: Administer an oral pain medication and leave the compress on
options.C: Remove the compress immediately and inspect the skin
options.D: Wait five minutes to see if the skin adjusts to the heat

explanation: If a patient says it burns, take it off right away and check the skin. Never ignore a burn complaint!

question: Which patient is the best candidate for a routine fasting blood sugar screening?

options.A: A young child recovering from a normal cold
options.B: A healthy athlete with mild muscle soreness after running
options.C: An adult with obesity and a family history of diabetes
options.D: An elderly patient admitted with a broken bone from a fall

explanation: Great thinking! People with risk factors like extra weight and a family history are prime candidates for routine checks so we catch issues early.

question: A patient comes in with swollen lower legs, brownish skin around the ankles, and a dull ache that gets worse when standing. What condition is most likely?

options.A: Raynaud's disease
options.B: Acute arterial blockage
options.C: Chronic venous insufficiency
options.D: Severe peripheral arterial disease

explanation: Those brownish marks, swelling, and tired aching legs are classic signs that blood is pooling in the lower legs because the veins are struggling to push it back up.

question: Why do fast-growing malignant tumors encourage angiogenesis (the growth of new blood vessels)?

options.A: It causes the tumor cells to mature and look normal
options.B: It stops the tumor from spreading to other organs
options.C: It helps cancer cells hide from white blood cells
options.D: It creates new blood vessels to supply oxygen and nutrients

explanation: Clever! Tumors need food and oxygen to keep growing rapidly. By triggering angiogenesis, they force the body to build a dedicated supply line straight to them.

question: What actually happens when a patient experiences hormone resistance?

options.A: Target cell receptors fail to respond to normal hormone levels
options.B: The pituitary gland blocks the bloodstream to the target tissue
options.C: The liver destroys circulating hormones before they reach organs
options.D: The endocrine gland completely stops producing all chemical messengers

explanation: Imagine knocking on a door (the hormone), but the doorbell is broken so nobody answers (the cell receptor). The hormone is present in the blood, but the cells just won't listen to it!

question: Why is an oxygen tent not the best choice when a patient needs very high oxygen levels?

options.A: The plastic material is chemically unable to hold high pressure
options.B: Opening the canopy to care for the patient causes the oxygen level to drop
options.C: Adults consume too much oxygen for the tent motor to handle
options.D: High oxygen levels melt the seals of the canopy frame

explanation: Every time you unzip or open the tent to check on the child or feed them, the trapped oxygen escapes quickly into the room air.

question: What safety step must you take immediately before moving a patient into a wheelchair?

options.A: Lock the wheels on both the bed and the wheelchair
options.B: Lower the wheelchair footrests permanently
options.C: Recline the wheelchair back completely flat
options.D: Remove the patient's identification band

explanation: Always lock those wheels! Unlocked furniture loves to roll away, which is a major cause of patient falls in the ward.

question: Why is a physical head-to-toe check important during a nutrition assessment?

options.A: It calculates the precise daily caloric expenditure during rest
options.B: It reveals visible deficiency signs like swollen gums or pale skin
options.C: It replaces the need for laboratory blood tests and dietary records
options.D: It accurately measures the exact percentage of body water volume

explanation: By simply looking at a patient's hair, skin, eyes, and mouth, you can often spot early physical clues of missing vitamins and minerals.

question: A patient with a suspected ectopic pregnancy complains of sudden, sharp pain in her right shoulder. Why does this happen?

options.A: Anxiety is causing muscle tension in her upper body.
options.B: Blood in her pelvis has irritated her diaphragm.
options.C: She strained her shoulder muscle while feeling dizzy.
options.D: An infection has spread upward to her lungs.

explanation: This is a classic nursing nugget! Blood pooling in the belly can irritate the phrenic nerve, which shares pathways with the shoulder. That's why pain shows up there!

question: During a community health screening, what is the most crucial infection control practice?

options.A: Cleaning stethoscope diaphragms and equipment between every client
options.B: Using disposable paper towels for hand drying only once a day
options.C: Wearing sterile surgical gowns for simple blood pressure checks
options.D: Keeping all the windows closed to prevent dust from entering

explanation: Spot on! Wiping down shared tools between patients is a simple habit that stops germs from spreading.

question: Which drug class is mainly used to calm down severe leprosy reactions and save nerves from permanent damage?

options.A: Antifungal agents
options.B: Broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.C: Corticosteroids
options.D: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs

explanation: Correct! Corticosteroids like prednisolone are superstars at calming down dangerous inflammation during leprosy flare-ups.

question: What is the primary receptor targeted by Class II antiarrhythmic drugs?

options.A: Calcium binding sites
options.B: Potassium ion channels
options.C: Beta-adrenergic receptors
options.D: Sodium transport gates

explanation: Class II drugs are beta-blockers that attach to beta-adrenergic receptors to block the effects of adrenaline on the heart. [learn more](GNS223_U1_T3#GNS223_U1_T3_h4)

question: A patient develops a fever, cough, and shortness of breath five days after being admitted to the surgical ward for a knee replacement. How is this infection classified?

options.A: Hospital-acquired pneumonia
options.B: Aspiration pneumonia
options.C: Community-acquired pneumonia
options.D: Primary acute bronchitis

explanation: Any pneumonia symptoms appearing 48 hours or longer after a patient is admitted to a healthcare facility are classified as hospital-acquired or nosocomial pneumonia. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h2)

question: A 25-year-old male client reports finding a hard, painless lump in his left testicle. What should the nurse suspect first?

options.A: Prostate adenocarcinoma
options.B: Testicular cancer
options.C: Benign prostatic hyperplasia
options.D: Renal cell carcinoma

explanation: Testicular cancer is most commonly seen in young adult men. A painless lump or swelling in the scrotum should always be checked out right away.

question: Which of these practices is DANGEROUS and should be avoided when writing dosages?

options.A: Writing out the word 'units' instead of abbreviations
options.B: Using a leading zero before a decimal (0.5 mg)
options.C: Using a trailing zero after a whole number (e.g., 5.0 mg)
options.D: Checking unfamiliar doses in a drug handbook

explanation: Never use trailing zeros! If the decimal point gets smudged, 5.0 mg can easily look like 50 mg. Keep it simple and safe (just write 5 mg).

question: What are the three small bones found inside the middle ear?

options.A: Tympanics
options.B: Cochlea
options.C: Turbinates
options.D: Ossicles

explanation: The malleus, incus, and stapes are collectively known as the ossicles, which transmit sound vibrations from the eardrum to the inner ear. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T5#GNS311_U3_T5_h1)

question: You find yourself treating a patient extra nicely just because they remind you of your sweet grandmother. What is this called?

options.A: Premature termination of the therapeutic phase
options.B: A failure in active listening techniques
options.C: Cultural stereotyping of the patient's background
options.D: Boundary crossing due to countertransference

explanation: Treating a patient differently because they remind you of someone in your personal life is a classic sign of countertransference clouding your professional judgment.

question: Why must a patient be fasting and completely rested when measuring true BMR?

options.A: To completely empty the bladder so body weight measurements stay accurate
options.B: To lower blood pressure enough to get an accurate electrical heart tracing
options.C: To prevent food digestion and physical activity from artificially raising the metabolic reading
options.D: To ensure the patient falls into a deep sleep during the diagnostic procedure

explanation: Even small movements or a recent meal can give your metabolism a temporary boost. To get a true baseline, we need the body completely quiet and digesting nothing!

question: Why is it so important to send a routine urine sample to the lab right away, or keep it in the fridge if there's a delay?

options.A: Prompt delivery prevents the patient from changing their mind about the test
options.B: Room temperature encourages bacterial growth and chemical breakdown
options.C: Leaving it out causes the plastic container to melt in warm rooms
options.D: Refrigeration speeds up the chemical reaction on dipstick pads

explanation: Urine left sitting in a warm room changes quickly—bacteria love to multiply in it, and cellular casts start to break apart, which ruins the accuracy of the test!

question: A community nurse notices women in a village avoiding breast screening due to cultural fears. What is the best way to handle this?

options.A: Report the village residents to local government authorities for non-compliance
options.B: Insist that screening is mandatory under all circumstances
options.C: Ignore the cultural beliefs and hand out clinical pamphlets silently
options.D: Provide culturally sensitive health education and address community fears openly

explanation: Spot on! Building trust through gentle, respectful conversations and addressing fears openly is always the best nursing approach for community health.

question: What is the most common active chemical found in modern spermicides?

options.A: Chlorhexidine
options.B: Hydrogen peroxide
options.C: Nonoxynol-9
options.D: Sodium hypochlorite

explanation: Correct! Nonoxynol-9 is the trusty chemical agent added to gels and foams to target and destroy sperm cell membranes.

question: In Nigeria, which official agency is responsible for receiving reports of adverse drug reactions?

options.A: FMOH
options.B: NAFDAC
options.C: NMA
options.D: NMCN

explanation: NAFDAC (National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control) is our national body that keeps watch over drug safety and collects these reports.

question: Which lab test specifically checks the extrinsic and common pathways of blood clotting?

options.A: Serum electrolyte panel
options.B: Complete blood count
options.C: Prothrombin Time (PT)
options.D: Blood urea nitrogen

explanation: PT is the go-to lab test to see how quickly the extrinsic pathway and common pathway are getting the job done.

question: Which of these is considered an extrinsic cause of a restrictive lung disease?

options.A: Chronic bronchitis from smoking
options.B: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
options.C: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
options.D: Severe scoliosis of the spine

explanation: You're doing awesome. 'Extrinsic' means the problem is outside the lung tissue itself—like a curved spine (scoliosis) squeezing the chest wall. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h5)

question: Which of the following is an example of an internalizing intentional injury?

options.A: Physical assault
options.B: Gang fighting
options.C: Suicide attempt
options.D: Armed robbery

explanation: Correct! Self-harm and suicide attempts are directed inward against oneself, which makes them internalizing intentional injuries.

question: How does linking daily unit goals to the bigger hospital mission help frontline nurses?

options.A: It isolates them from the rest of the healthcare team.
options.B: It gives them a sense of purpose by connecting daily work to the wider mission.
options.C: It forces them to perform administrative duties instead of patient care.
options.D: It decreases their responsibility for patient safety outcomes.

explanation: It feels great to know that your busy shift on the ward is actually part of something much bigger and meaningful for patient care!

question: What is a vital safety question a nurse must ask a young female patient before a pelvic or abdominal X-ray?

options.A: Do you have a history of high blood pressure?
options.B: Have you ever had a blood transfusion?
options.C: Could you possibly be pregnant?
options.D: What is your normal daily diet?

explanation: Radiation can harm a growing baby, so checking for pregnancy beforehand is a crucial safety step for every female of childbearing age.

question: Which specific hormone surge directly triggers the release of the egg from the ovary?

options.A: Oxytocin
options.B: Progesterone
options.C: Luteinizing hormone
options.D: Prolactin

explanation: A sharp peak in luteinizing hormone is the exact physiological trigger that causes the follicle to burst and release the egg. [learn more](GNS216_U2_T3#GNS216_U2_T3_h4)

question: If an older male patient has an enlarged prostate (BPH), what urinary symptom is he most likely to complain about?

options.A: A weak and slow urinary stream
options.B: Total absence of urine production
options.C: Inability to control bowel movements
options.D: Severe pain during bladder filling

explanation: Makes total sense, right? When the prostate grows, it presses on the urethra like a pinched garden hose, making the urine flow slow and weak.

question: Which type of tongue bumps (papillae) do NOT have any taste buds?

options.A: Filiform papillae
options.B: Fungiform papillae
options.C: Vallate papillae
options.D: Foliate papillae

explanation: Filiform papillae are the rough little bumps that give your tongue friction to help grip food—they aren't involved in tasting.

question: Up to how many days after childbirth can a mother's death still be classified as maternal mortality?

options.A: Ninety days
options.B: Forty-two days
options.C: Seven days
options.D: Fourteen days

explanation: You've got this! Officially, maternal death includes any death during pregnancy or within 42 days (6 weeks) after delivery. Keep that timeline in mind!

question: Why does chronic kidney disease often lead to secondary hyperparathyroidism?

options.A: Urine output drops so low that calcium crystallizes inside the bladder.
options.B: Failing kidneys cannot activate vitamin D or clear phosphate properly.
options.C: The kidneys start producing parathyroid hormone in place of the glands.
options.D: Renal failure directly destroys all four parathyroid glands within weeks.

explanation: When kidneys fail, they struggle to clear phosphate and activate vitamin D, which drops your calcium levels and forces the parathyroid glands to work overtime.

question: What is a major benefit of putting a newborn straight onto the mother's chest for skin-to-skin contact?

options.A: It stabilizes the infant's body temperature and heart rate
options.B: It completely eliminates the need for vitamin K injections
options.C: It speeds up the closure of the umbilical cord vessels
options.D: It prevents the occurrence of physiological jaundice

explanation: Mum's chest is like a natural incubator! It helps steady the baby's breathing, heart rate, and keeps them nice and warm.

question: What is the main job of the mucosa, the innermost layer of your gut?

options.A: Providing outer structural protection
options.B: Secreting mucus and absorbing nutrients
options.C: Generating rhythmic muscular contractions
options.D: Anchoring the tract to the abdominal wall

explanation: You've got this! The mucosa faces right inside the tube, making it our body's frontline hero for soaking up nutrients and keeping things slippery with mucus.

question: What is the primary benefit of enrolling a patient in a structured cardiac rehabilitation program?

options.A: Providing a surgical alternative to coronary artery bypass grafting
options.B: Improving overall physical conditioning and reducing future heart risks
options.C: Ensuring the patient never has to take prescription medications again
options.D: Eliminating the need for routine follow-up visits with the cardiologist

explanation: Cardiac rehabilitation helps patients regain strength, manage risk factors, lower stress, and significantly reduce the likelihood of future cardiac events. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T13#GNS213_U1_T13_h6)

question: Why is a continuous flow of saliva important for maintaining oral health?

options.A: It lubricates food, aids digestion, and protects teeth by controlling bacteria.
options.B: It acts as the primary hormone regulating blood sugar levels after a heavy meal.
options.C: It supplies the stomach with the strong acid required to kill swallowed parasites.
options.D: It absorbs excess dietary fats before they can reach the small intestine.

explanation: Saliva does much more than help us swallow; its protective enzymes and antibodies actively fight off harmful bacteria in the mouth. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T1#GNS121_U1_T1_h5)

question: Which medication class is most commonly associated with causing orthostatic fainting?

options.A: Antacids
options.B: Antihypertensives
options.C: Antibiotics
options.D: Analgesics

explanation: Medications that lower blood pressure can sometimes drop it too far, especially when standing up, leading to fainting. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T16#GNS123_U3_T16_h3)

question: Why are heart-rhythm medications often stopped before an EPS?

options.A: To keep the access site veins from collapsing during catheter insertion
options.B: To allow doctors to successfully provoke the abnormal heart rhythm
options.C: To prevent the patient from falling asleep during the procedure
options.D: To lower the patient's baseline blood pressure safely

explanation: It sounds backwards, but doctors actually *want* to see the bad rhythm happen so they can fix it. If the antiarrhythmic drugs are working too well, they might hide the problem during the test!

question: During post-mortem care, why is a small pillow placed under the patient's head?

options.A: To prevent blood pooling and discoloration in the face
options.B: To make it easier to attach mechanical ventilators
options.C: To ensure the jaw stays wide open for viewing
options.D: To keep the patient comfortable during sleep cycles

explanation: Great job! Raising the head slightly stops gravity from pooling blood in the face, keeping a natural look.

question: How does missing one fallopian tube generally affect a woman's chances of getting pregnant naturally?

options.A: The patient will instantly experience early surgical menopause
options.B: Pregnancy is still possible because the remaining tube can function
options.C: Natural conception is completely impossible without medical help
options.D: Ectopic pregnancies will occur in every single attempted cycle

explanation: Wonderful news for patients! One healthy tube is often all it takes to capture an egg and achieve a natural pregnancy.

question: Why is carbidopa always given alongside levodopa when treating Parkinson's?

options.A: To act as a direct replacement for lost acetylcholine
options.B: To sedate the patient and prevent involuntary tremors
options.C: To prevent the breakdown of levodopa before it reaches the brain
options.D: To completely cure the underlying neuronal degeneration

explanation: Think of carbidopa as the bodyguard for levodopa. It stops levodopa from breaking down too early in the body so that enough of it actually reaches the brain to do its job!

question: What is the name of the smooth, triangular area found on the inner floor of the bladder?

options.A: The renal pelvis
options.B: The meatus
options.C: The glomerulus
options.D: The trigone

explanation: It's called the trigone (think 'triangle'). It is marked out by the openings of your two ureters and your urethra, and germs love to hang out here during bladder infections.

question: What important clinical step must a nurse take before starting a returning defaulter on a new hormonal contraceptive?

options.A: Require the client to pay a fine for defaulting
options.B: Wait for laboratory tests that take three weeks
options.C: Carefully rule out existing pregnancy
options.D: Consult the national ministry of health directly

explanation: Safety first! Always rule out pregnancy before dispensing or administering new hormonal methods to protect both client and baby.

question: Why must you always check the meal tray against the patient's diet ticket before feeding?

options.A: To calculate the exact financial cost of the hospital meal
options.B: To check if the kitchen included extra dessert for the nurse
options.C: To measure the exact weight of the food for hospital records
options.D: To confirm the correct food consistency and dietary restrictions

explanation: Spot-checking the diet ticket is a key safety habit. It ensures your patient gets the right textures—like pureed foods when needed—preventing dangerous mix-ups.

question: Why are patients usually asked to hold their breath for a quick second during a chest X-ray?

options.A: To prevent radiation from entering the stomach
options.B: To prevent motion blur and clearly view lung fields
options.C: To lower their blood pressure during the flash
options.D: To make the heart beat slower for the picture

explanation: Breathing makes the chest move, which blurs the picture. Holding still gives us a crystal-clear image!

question: What does the term 'cachexia' mean in advanced illness?

options.A: A sudden increase in daily appetite
options.B: Complete blockage of the large intestine
options.C: An infection caused by poor dental hygiene
options.D: Severe muscle wasting and weight loss

explanation: You've got this! Cachexia is a whole-body wasting condition caused by disease inflammation, not just because the person isn't eating enough food.

question: As a nurse, you notice some IV fluid bottles on the ward shelf have changed color and passed their expiry date. What should you do?

options.A: Take the bottles home to use for domestic cleaning purposes
options.B: Hide the expired bottles in a bottom drawer so nobody notices
options.C: Administer them quickly to unsuspecting patients before they worsen
options.D: Report the expired stock immediately according to facility protocol

explanation: Safety first! Reporting expired stock keeps patients safe and ensures losses are recorded properly instead of silently disappearing.

question: Why are spinal reflexes important for the body?

options.A: They allow the brain to store long-term memories of painful events
options.B: They control conscious decisions made during physical exercise
options.C: They circulate nutrients through the spinal canal
options.D: They provide rapid, automatic responses without waiting for brain processing

explanation: Reflexes bypass the brain to react instantly to danger, such as pulling a hand away from a hot stove. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h3)

question: Which genetic marker is closely linked with ankylosing spondylitis?

options.A: HLA-B27
options.B: CD4
options.C: RH factor
options.D: BRCA1

explanation: Keep this gene in mind: HLA-B27 is strongly tied to ankylosing spondylitis, a condition that mainly stiffens up the spine.

question: What is the emergency reversal drug given during a dangerous opioid overdose?

options.A: Protamine sulfate
options.B: Atropine
options.C: Naloxone
options.D: Vitamin K

explanation: Naloxone is a lifesaver! It bumps opioids off their receptors in a hurry and helps the patient breathe again.

question: What is the best way to report a patient's death when calling the doctor?

options.A: Provide a concise report of assessment findings and absent vital signs
options.B: Wait until the morning shift change before making the phone call
options.C: Ask the physician for permission to start post-mortem care immediately
options.D: Ask the doctor to sign the death certificate over the telephone

explanation: Well done! Giving quick, clear facts helps the doctor understand what's happening before they even step into the room.

question: Why must emergency airway and suction equipment always be kept ready at the bedside during intrapleural procedures?

options.A: To test the electrical outlets in the hospital room
options.B: To manage sudden respiratory distress or acute complications quickly
options.C: To clean out the chest drainage canister every single hour
options.D: To routinely suction excess saliva from the patient's mouth

explanation: Always expect the unexpected! Because chest procedures can sometimes cause sudden breathing changes, having emergency gear ready keeps your patient safe.

question: A patient worries that a missing fallopian tube means she can never have a family. What is the best initial nursing response?

options.A: Immediately refer her to a psychiatric hospital for intensive inpatient therapy
options.B: Explain that her general health is ruined and she must accept childlessness
options.C: Tell her not to worry because most women never want children anyway
options.D: Listen empathetically, validate her feelings, and explain available fertility options like IVF

explanation: You're a caring nurse! Combining a listening ear with reassuring medical facts helps ease her mind and points her toward real solutions.

question: Why do doctors order an MRI or CT scan for a patient suspected of having GPI?

options.A: To check the exact amount of bacteria floating in the blood
options.B: To see how well the patient's body handles penicillin
options.C: To check for brain shrinkage and rule out other causes of dementia
options.D: To prove the patient has a brand-new skin sore from syphilis

explanation: You got it! Brain scans help us spot shrinkage (atrophy) and make sure the symptoms aren't coming from a stroke, tumor, or other memory issues.

question: What is the main thing you do during the evaluation phase of the nursing process?

options.A: Gathering initial demographic data during the patient's admission
options.B: Writing out shift handoff notes without checking patient progress
options.C: Comparing the patient's actual health status against the expected outcomes
options.D: Formulating brand new medical diagnoses for the physician to sign

explanation: Evaluation is like checking your scorecard. You look back at the goals you set and ask, 'Did our care help the patient reach them?'

question: Which of these activities is a great example of 'mutual aid'?

options.A: Neighbors contributing money to pay for a sick person's hospital bill
options.B: A police officer giving a traffic ticket to a speeding driver
options.C: A commercial bank approving a business loan for a farmer
options.D: A teacher giving a graded examination to students in a school

explanation: Spot on! Mutual aid happens when community members voluntarily join hands to support someone who is sick or in need.

question: Why are vitamins and minerals called essential micronutrients?

options.A: The human liver can easily manufacture them if the diet lacks variety.
options.B: They are the main source of daily calories and tissue bulk in the diet.
options.C: They are only needed during times of severe illness or physical injury.
options.D: The body needs them in small amounts and cannot produce enough on its own.

explanation: Brilliant! 'Micro' means we only need tiny amounts, but 'essential' means our bodies can't make them—so we must get them from our food. Easy peasy!

question: Which lifestyle advice is most important for a nurse to emphasize during patient education for sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Restrict fluid intake in the evening to prevent frequent nighttime urination
options.B: Maintain consistent daily hydration and avoid extreme temperature changes
options.C: Wear tight, supportive clothing to keep the peripheral blood vessels compressed
options.D: Engage in intense competitive sports to build strong cardiovascular endurance

explanation: Drinking plenty of water prevents the blood from thickening, and avoiding cold temperatures stops blood vessels from narrowing, both of which prevent crises. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h7)

question: What is the main reason for doing routine physical stock counts in a pharmacy?

options.A: To compare actual physical inventory with financial records
options.B: To calculate the annual salary bonus for the nursing staff
options.C: To return all expired items directly to government ministers
options.D: To increase the retail price of all fast-moving medications

explanation: Stock counts help catch errors, missing items, or record mistakes early, making sure the physical drugs match what the books say.

question: What is an important long-term instruction for a patient who just received a mechanical heart valve?

options.A: Never drinking pure water again
options.B: Avoiding all forms of physical movement forever
options.C: Stopping daily blood pressure checks at home
options.D: The need for lifelong anticoagulation therapy

explanation: Blood loves to stick to artificial surfaces! Patients with mechanical valves must take blood thinners (anticoagulants) for the rest of their lives to prevent dangerous clots.

question: Why is a patient usually asked to lie flat after a lumbar puncture?

options.A: To help prevent a low-pressure spinal headache
options.B: To speed up the absorption of the local anesthetic
options.C: To keep the blood pressure from dropping too fast
options.D: To prevent the collection tubes from falling over

explanation: Correct! Lying flat reduces pull on the meninges where the needle went in, lowering the chance of a terrible headache.

question: Between these two types of mouth lesions, which one carries a higher risk of turning into cancer?

options.A: Erythroplakia
options.B: Aphthous ulcer
options.C: Herpes labialis
options.D: Leukoplakia

explanation: Erythroplakia shows up as red, velvety patches and is much more likely to become malignant compared to white patches (leukoplakia).

question: Why do doctors prescribe a combination of different HIV drugs instead of just one?

options.A: To eliminate the need for routine laboratory viral load testing
options.B: To ensure the patient has fewer daily pills to swallow
options.C: To completely cure the patient of the infection within weeks
options.D: To prevent the virus from quickly mutating and developing drug resistance

explanation: Exactly! Hitting the virus from multiple angles makes it super hard for it to mutate and find a way around the medication.

question: Which team member helps a patient regain fine motor skills for daily dressing and eating?

options.A: Physiotherapist
options.B: Occupational therapist
options.C: Medical social worker
options.D: Speech-language pathologist

explanation: Occupational therapists (OTs) focus on everyday activities and hand coordination, while physiotherapists focus more on walking and big movements.

question: Which lab tests are most important to monitor regularly for patients taking long-term multi-drug therapy?

options.A: Liver enzymes and kidney function tests
options.B: Stool culture and electrolyte balance
options.C: Thyroid hormones and iron levels
options.D: Complete blood count and blood type

explanation: Spot on! Since the liver and kidneys do the heavy lifting of processing and clearing drugs, keeping an eye on their lab values is our best way to catch early signs of strain or toxicity.

question: What should you do if a doctor's written order is messy or unclear?

options.A: Guess based on the diagnosis
options.B: Give half the dose just to be safe
options.C: Ask another patient in the ward
options.D: Call the prescriber directly to clarify

explanation: Never guess! Always contact the doctor who wrote the order to clear up any confusion before giving the drug.

question: Why is knowing the exact route abbreviation so important for safe medication delivery?

options.A: It determines how fast the drug works and prevents wrong-route errors
options.B: It replaces the need to check the patient's identity band
options.C: It decides which nurse is legally permitted to touch the patient
options.D: It tells the nurse the exact financial cost of the medication supply

explanation: Spot on! Different routes change how quickly a drug enters the bloodstream. Getting the route wrong can lead to serious patient harm, so always double-check!

question: What is the main purpose of 'comfort feeding' in palliative care?

options.A: Maximizing pleasure and honoring patient preferences
options.B: Lowering blood pressure through low-salt choices
options.C: Strictly controlling blood sugar levels
options.D: Reversing severe malnutrition over time

explanation: Spot on! Comfort feeding means throwing out strict diet rules so the patient can simply enjoy their favorite tastes and feel happy.

question: Why do dying patients often get cool, pale, and mottled hands and feet?

options.A: Lack of oxygen forces the lungs to shut down blood flow to the limbs
options.B: Kidney failure causes excess fluid to accumulate under the skin layers
options.C: The patient is experiencing a sudden and severe drop in environmental temperature
options.D: The heart loses the ability to pump blood effectively to peripheral tissues

explanation: As the body slows down, it naturally prioritizes sending blood to vital organs like the brain and heart, leaving the hands and feet cool to the touch.

question: Which hormone is mainly responsible for growing and branching the milk ducts during early development?

options.A: Estrogen
options.B: Oxytocin
options.C: Progesterone
options.D: Prolactin

explanation: Estrogen acts like the master gardener, helping the milk duct system grow and branch out nicely inside the breast.

question: Why does a low CD4 count cause the whole immune system to fail?

options.A: CD4 cells seal the lymphatic vessels to trap invading bacteria
options.B: CD4 cells directly produce all the red blood cells in the body
options.C: CD4 cells act as master coordinators that activate other immune cells
options.D: CD4 cells form a physical barrier around organs to block viruses

explanation: Brilliant! CD4 helper cells are like the generals in an army—without them, the rest of the immune defenses don't know how to fight back. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h6)

question: Why is the term 'youth' viewed more as a social stage rather than just a fixed age group?

options.A: It only applies to individuals living in urban environments
options.B: It focuses heavily on social roles, independence, and economic status
options.C: It is determined entirely by the onset of puberty hormones
options.D: It is a fixed medical diagnosis made by physicians

explanation: 'Youth' is all about moving into the adult world—finding work, gaining independence, and taking on new social responsibilities.

question: What does male sexual dysfunction mainly affect?

options.A: Upper respiratory function
options.B: Physical intimacy and satisfaction
options.C: Renal filtration capacity
options.D: Skeletal muscle development

explanation: You've got this! Male sexual dysfunction simply means there's trouble with enjoying or engaging in sexual activity. It's all about intimacy and satisfaction.

question: Why might a PET scan sometimes show a false-positive result for a patient who does not have cancer?

options.A: The radioactive tracer naturally binds to healthy muscle tissue over time.
options.B: Fasting before the test forces normal cells to mimic cancerous growth.
options.C: Dehydration causes the scanner to misread shadows as malignant tumors.
options.D: Inflammation and infection can also cause high glucose uptake in tissues.

explanation: Spot on! White blood cells fighting an infection also need lots of glucose, meaning an ordinary infection or inflammation can sometimes 'light up' on a PET scan just like a tumor would.

question: Which vaccine is given to a newborn right at birth to protect against tuberculosis?

options.A: BCG
options.B: Yellow fever
options.C: Measles
options.D: Tetanus toxoid

explanation: Spot on! BCG is one of those precious birth-dose vaccines given before baby leaves the health facility.

question: Which of these is a main goal of doing passive range of motion?

options.A: Increasing active muscle strength
options.B: Lowering high blood pressure instantly
options.C: Keeping joint flexibility and movement
options.D: Treating underlying bone infections

explanation: Well done! Passive movements are specifically designed to keep joints flexible when a patient cannot move themselves.

question: What is the key job of the special fluid called surfactant in your lungs?

options.A: To reduce surface tension and prevent alveolar collapse
options.B: To bind oxygen molecules directly for transport
options.C: To moisten the trachea and primary bronchi
options.D: To trap dust and bacteria entering the deep lungs

explanation: Brilliant! Surfactant keeps the tiny air sacs from sticking together and collapsing on themselves when you breathe out.

question: Which symptom is most characteristic of thyroid hormone hypersecretion?

options.A: Rapid weight loss and heat intolerance
options.B: Yellowing of the skin and dark urine
options.C: Low blood pressure and extreme fatigue
options.D: Severe weight gain and cold intolerance

explanation: Too much thyroid hormone speeds up the body's metabolism, causing patients to burn energy fast, lose weight, and feel very hot. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T7#GNS211_U1_T7_h3)

question: What is the main difference between routine blood typing and a cross-match?

options.A: Blood typing requires samples from both the donor and recipient families
options.B: Cross-matching tests for hidden incompatibilities beyond basic ABO and Rh types
options.C: Cross-matching measures the exact amount of oxygen in donor plasma
options.D: Blood typing is only performed after a transfusion has already started

explanation: Cross-matching is a direct laboratory test that checks for reactions against minor antigens that standard typing misses. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h5)

question: Why is it smart to check that gas is actually flowing out of the cannula prongs before placing them on the patient?

options.A: To measure the exact oxygen percentage in the room air
options.B: To confirm the equipment works and gas is actively delivering
options.C: To clear out any trapped dust from the manufacturing factory
options.D: To warm up the cold gas before it touches the sensitive nasal lining

explanation: A quick check saves a lot of trouble—you want to make sure there isn't a kinked tube or a closed valve blocking air before it reaches your patient.

question: Why is checking blood sugar one of the first things to do when caring for an unresponsive patient?

options.A: Hypoglycemia is a metabolic cause of altered consciousness that can be quickly reversed
options.B: Glucose checks replace the need for a neurological exam
options.C: High blood sugar directly damages the brainstem within minutes
options.D: Diabetes mellitus is the primary cause of all neurological trauma

explanation: Spot on! Low blood sugar starves the brain of energy, causing unconsciousness that can fix itself almost instantly once glucose is given.

question: Which of the following is NOT a common challenge facing DRF exemptions in public hospitals?

options.A: Persistent stockouts caused by lack of reimbursement
options.B: Bureaucratic delays in patient verification
options.C: Exploitation of loopholes by non-indigent individuals
options.D: Excessive government funding that overflows the pharmacy

explanation: If only! Public hospitals rarely have excessive funding; instead, they constantly battle underfunding and delayed subventions.

question: What is 'primary non-fulfillment' when talking about medication adherence?

options.A: The patient forgets to take afternoon doses only
options.B: The patient stops taking drugs after feeling better
options.C: The patient never fills or picks up the new prescription
options.D: The patient cuts their pills in half to save money

explanation: Think of it as step one: they leave the clinic with a script, but never actually buy or pick up the medicine.

question: As a nurse, what is your very first priority when a patient arrives with complications from an abortion?

options.A: Filing a formal police report immediately
options.B: Evaluating vital signs for shock and stability
options.C: Asking about her religious and marital status
options.D: Conducting a detailed financial background check

explanation: Safety first! Always check vital signs and stabilize the patient first to prevent life-threatening shock or heavy bleeding.

question: What is the primary physical change that happens first in a joint affected by osteoarthritis?

options.A: Swelling of the surrounding muscles
options.B: Infection of the synovial fluid
options.C: Breakdown of articular cartilage
options.D: Fusion of the two bone ends

explanation: Osteoarthritis starts when the protective cartilage covering the ends of bones begins to wear away and break down. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T14#GNS222_U1_T14_h1)

question: How should you clean a patient's skin before giving an injection?

options.A: Wiping in a circular motion from the center outward and letting it dry
options.B: Applying an antiseptic spray and immediately inserting the needle
options.C: Wiping from the outer edges inward toward the center of the site
options.D: Scrubbing vigorously back and forth with a dry cotton ball

explanation: Always move from clean (center) to less clean (outward) to push germs away. Plus, letting the alcohol dry is what actually kills the microbes!

question: Which sign tells you that a limb in traction has poor blood flow?

options.A: The ability to wiggle all toes easily on command
options.B: Cold toes and a slow capillary refill over four seconds
options.C: Warm skin and a strong pulse in the foot
options.D: Normal pink coloration of the nail beds

explanation: Great job thinking through circulation checks! Cold toes and sluggish refill are classic warning signs that pressure or swelling is slowing down blood flow.

question: Why should nurses care about why patients stay silent when safety rules are skipped?

options.A: It reduces the need to sterilize reusable equipment
options.B: Patients are usually at fault for bad clinical outcomes
options.C: It proves that hospitals have enough medical supplies
options.D: Understanding patient silence helps nurses improve safety advocacy

explanation: You got it! When we understand why patients keep quiet, we can break those barriers and speak up better for their safety.

question: What food safety rule is most important for a patient with a severely weakened immune system?

options.A: Eat only thoroughly cooked foods and avoid raw fruits or unpasteurized dairy
options.B: Consume raw salads daily to increase natural vitamin and fiber intake
options.C: Eat street foods as long as they are served at room temperature
options.D: Drink fresh unpasteurized milk to boost beneficial gut bacteria

explanation: You got it! Raw foods and unpasteurized dairy can hide sneaky bacteria and parasites that a healthy body handles easily, but can overwhelm a weak immune system.

question: What is the main difference between an intermittent fever and a remittent fever?

options.A: Remittent causes chills, while intermittent only causes sweating
options.B: Remittent only happens at night, while intermittent has no schedule
options.C: Intermittent drops back to normal daily, while remittent stays high even though it fluctuates
options.D: Intermittent lasts for weeks, while remittent goes away in hours

explanation: Well done! The big clue is whether the temperature touches the normal baseline at least once during the day.

question: What is a major risk or downside if team leadership on the ward is weak?

options.A: Patients refusing to take any hospital medications
options.B: Automatic promotion of all junior staff members
options.C: Blurred responsibilities and fragmented patient care
options.D: Doctors taking over all nursing responsibilities

explanation: That's right! When leadership lacks clear direction, team members get confused about who is supposed to do what, leading to gaps in patient care.

question: Why do nurses group skin problems into categories like 'inflammatory' or 'autoimmune'?

options.A: To avoid performing physical assessments on patients with open lesions
options.B: To determine the exact financial cost of required pharmaceutical treatments
options.C: To prove that every skin condition shares the exact same cellular origin
options.D: To quickly understand the underlying cause and guide general nursing care

explanation: Spot on! Classifying skin issues helps you anticipate how a disease will act so you can plan the best nursing care.

question: A client with an inherited degenerative disorder shows early muscle weakness and clumsy coordination. What should you do first?

options.A: Prepare the client for emergency surgery to repair the damaged genes
options.B: Document the findings, report the progression to the healthcare team, and assess safety needs
options.C: Tell the family that these mild symptoms will completely disappear within a week
options.D: Advise the client to stop all physical movement immediately to prevent further weakness

explanation: Spotting these changes early and planning for safety helps protect the client from falls as their motor skills decline.

question: Why do oral rehydration solutions (ORS) mix both salt (sodium) and sugar (glucose) together?

options.A: Sodium prevents the sugar from causing high blood pressure
options.B: Sugar masks the unpleasant salty taste of the solution
options.C: Glucose gives the patient immediate energy to walk around
options.D: Glucose helps transport sodium and water across the intestinal wall

explanation: It's a brilliant biological team-up! Glucose acts like a VIP ticket, helping the intestines pull sodium—and water right along with it—back into the bloodstream.

question: Why do intramuscular (IM) injections absorb faster than subcutaneous ones?

options.A: Muscle tissue has a much richer blood supply
options.B: The skin barrier is thinner over muscle sites
options.C: Injections into muscle bypass the liver completely
options.D: Needles used for muscle are always smaller

explanation: Think of blood vessels as busy highways! Because muscles have way more blood vessels than fatty tissue underneath the skin, the medicine gets swept right up into the bloodstream much faster.

question: Which specific lobe of the brain houses the primary motor cortex?

options.A: Frontal lobe
options.B: Occipital lobe
options.C: Parietal lobe
options.D: Temporal lobe

explanation: Great recall! The primary motor cortex lives right in the frontal lobe, specifically in the precentral gyrus.

question: Why must a nurse know the specific type of FGM a patient has experienced?

options.A: It determines the appropriate legal fine for the family
options.B: It dictates the patient's future career choices
options.C: It guides the exact surgical and obstetric management needed
options.D: It predicts the exact age when the procedure was done

explanation: Spot on! Different types involve different levels of tissue removal, which tells you what kind of clinical care or surgery she might need. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T8#GNS312_U1_T8_h1)

question: Why is a luminal medication also prescribed along with tissue-active drugs?

options.A: To replace lost electrolytes and boost red blood cell production
options.B: To permanently numb the lining of the stomach against acid
options.C: To speed up the healing of skin lesions on the abdomen
options.D: To clear remaining cysts from the bowel lumen and prevent relapse

explanation: Exactly! While one drug clears the tissues, the luminal agent mops up any cysts left in the gut so the infection doesn't bounce back.

question: Why do doctors often use numbing spray and a nasal decongestant before a flexible scope goes into the nose?

options.A: To numb the passage, reduce discomfort, and shrink mucosal tissues for easier scope entry
options.B: To dilate the pupils so the patient can see the monitor during the examination
options.C: To put the patient into a deep sleep and prevent sudden body movements
options.D: To relax the heart rate and lower the patient's resting blood pressure

explanation: Spot on! The nose and throat are very sensitive, so numbing and shrinking the tissues makes the scope slide in much more comfortably.
